# How to Write a Simple Cover Letter When You Have No Idea Where to Start

> **In short:** A cover letter is a short note (three short paragraphs) that explains who you are, why you want the job, and what you bring. You don't need years of experience — you just need a simple formula and a few honest sentences.

Staring at a blank page is the hardest part. Most people think a cover letter has to sound impressive, formal, or full of achievements. It doesn't. A hiring manager wants to know three things: who you are, why this job caught your eye, and why you're worth a quick chat. This guide gives you a repeating three-paragraph formula that works even when you feel you have nothing to say. By the end, you'll have a first draft you can save as a template and reuse.

## Before you start
- **A job posting** (or two) you want to apply to — keep it open while you write.
- **A notes app or blank document** on your phone or computer (Google Docs, Notes, Word — anything works).
- **About 30 to 45 minutes.** You don't have to finish in one sitting; saving halfway is fine.
- No paid tools or accounts are needed for this guide. If you want help polishing the wording later, you can paste your draft into an AI assistant like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini — but the writing itself starts with you.

## Step 1 — Open with one clear sentence about who you are
Start a new document and write the first sentence as a simple introduction: your name (or "I'm [name]"), what you're looking for, and one small honest detail. Think of this first sentence as your handshake across the table — short, friendly, and clear. After you type it, you'll see your draft begin to take shape instead of staying an empty white page.
💬 Example: "I'm Maria, and I'm applying for the assistant coordinator role at Greenleaf Studio."
If you don't know what to call yourself yet, just write "I'm applying for the [job title] role at [company]" and fill the blanks in later. You'll know it worked when you have a single confident opening line you can read out loud without cringing.

## Step 2 — Add one paragraph about why this job, this company
Now write two or three sentences answering: what about this job posting pulled you in, and what do you already know or like about the company? Don't fake passion — pick one real, small reason. Maybe it's the product they make, a value they mentioned in the posting, or simply that the role fits your schedule. This paragraph is your chance to sound like a real person, not a template.
💬 Example: "I've been following Greenleaf for about a year — I love how their weekly newsletter explains design ideas in plain language. The assistant role looks like a good fit because the hours match my study schedule and I get to write, which is what I enjoy most."
If your reason feels too small, write it anyway. Hiring managers read hundreds of generic letters; a small honest reason stands out. You'll know it worked when you can finish the sentence "I'm interested in this role because…" without hesitating.

## Step 3 — Write one paragraph about what you bring, even without experience
This is the part most people freeze on, so here's the trick: pick two or three concrete things you can do (school projects, volunteering, a part-time job, helping family, a hobby) and connect each one to a task in the job posting. The job posting is a list of hints — every line that says "we need someone who…" is a clue for what to mention. "No experience" usually means "I haven't had this exact job title," not "I have nothing useful to offer."
💬 Example: "Last summer I helped organize a school fundraiser, which involved replying to emails, keeping a small spreadsheet of donations, and giving short updates at weekly meetings. I also write a personal blog where I edit my own drafts, so I'm comfortable rewriting text until it sounds right. Both feel close to what the assistant coordinator role does day to day."
If you truly can't think of anything, write about how you learn: a class you took, a tutorial you finished, even a YouTube video that taught you a new skill. You'll know it worked when you can point to two or three real moments in your past and connect each to a sentence in the job posting.

## Step 4 — Close with a short, friendly ending
End the letter with two or three sentences: thank the reader for their time, say you'd welcome a chat, and sign off politely. Think of this as the moment you stand up, smile, and walk out of the room — leave a good feeling behind. Don't add new information here; just wrap up.
💬 Example: "Thanks for reading — I'd love to chat about how I could help at Greenleaf. I'm available weekdays after 4pm and can be reached at maria@example.com."
If you don't know the hiring manager's name, "Dear Hiring Manager," or "Hi Greenleaf team," both work — don't stress over the perfect greeting. You'll know it worked when the letter feels complete and you'd be comfortable sending it today.

## Step 5 — Trim and read it out loud
Cut anything that repeats a point you already made, and remove long words where a short one works. Read the whole letter out loud, slowly — your ear catches stiff or robotic sentences faster than your eye does. Anywhere you stumble, rewrite that sentence the way you'd actually say it to a friend. Aim for one page (roughly 250–350 words total).
💬 Example: change "I am writing to express my interest in the position of assistant coordinator" to "I'm applying for the assistant coordinator role." Same meaning, half the weight.
If you're over one page, you almost certainly repeated yourself in Step 2 or Step 3 — cut the weakest sentence in each. You'll know it worked when the whole letter reads smoothly out loud in under a minute.

## Step 6 — Save the file with a clear name and reuse the template
Save your finished letter as something easy to find, like `cover-letter-greenleaf-v1.docx`, then keep it open as your base template. For your next application, copy the file, swap in the new company name and the two or three points that match the new posting, and you're most of the way there. The formula stays the same — only the details change.
💬 Example: copy the file to `cover-letter-riverside-cafe-v1.docx`, then update the company name, the "why this job" paragraph, and one or two examples in the "what I bring" paragraph.
If you ever get stuck on a new posting, return to Step 3 and re-read it with the new job description in hand — the posting always tells you what to write. You'll know it worked when you can produce a new first draft in under 20 minutes.

## Common mistakes
- **Writing a full life story.** Keep it to three short paragraphs plus a sign-off. Anything longer buries the point and the hiring manager will skim past it. The fix: paste your draft into a word counter — if it's over 350 words, cut the least important sentence in each paragraph.
- **Copy-pasting the same letter to every job.** Hiring managers spot generic letters instantly, and they often end up ignored. The fix: keep your template, but always rewrite Step 2 and Step 3 so they mention the specific company and the specific posting — that alone makes you stand out.
- **Trying to sound "professional" by using stiff, formal language.** Long words and stiff phrases make your letter feel cold and harder to read. The fix: write the way you talk, then read it out loud in Step 5 — wherever you stumble, simplify. A friendly, clear letter beats a fancy, confusing one every time.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the three-paragraph formula is useful far beyond job hunting — it works for introduction emails, scholarship requests, and even short messages to a landlord or a school. Once you have it, you'll reach for it again and again.
- **For your business or work:** if you ever freelance, pitch a service, or apply for internal promotions, the same shape applies: who you are, why this specific opportunity, what you bring, close. Keep the template somewhere safe.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is to apply the formula to a job you already like the sound of, even if you don't send the application yet. Drafting the letter itself is the practice — sending it is optional.

## Try it now
Open a blank document, type a single sentence with your name and the job you're applying for, and stop there. That's Step 1 done. The rest of the letter is just three more short paragraphs using the same recipe.
